source.title: Towards Robust Model Organisms for Eliciting Latent Knowledge
source.authors: Lennart Finke; Hardik Bhatnagar; Euodia Dodd; Francis Rhys Ward; Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye; Matthias Bethge; Mary Phuong

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies weak-to-strong fine-tuning as an elicitation attack and reports vulnerability recall afterward, but does not use the original PGR measure or compare against a strong model trained on true labels.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is the weak-to-strong (WtS) training condition in Table 4, with related stepwise results described and plotted in Figure 3d. Other elicitation protocols and unrelated capability evaluations are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes stronger models on a weaker model's (T, Qwen3-8B) vulnerability-task responses and reports their hard-sample recall against T's own recall. This bears on V1 in a new setting: eliciting capability from sandbagging model organisms and a plain strong base model. It is T3 rather than T2: the question is capability elicitation, there is no PGR, and no true-label ceiling. The sandbagging is induced on purpose, but the weak-to-strong effect itself is not, so the WtS results still bear on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors call fine-tuning on T's hard-sample completions the most effective attack they tested. One or two steps with two samples each elicit nonzero correct-solution rates from all reference organisms. Their Stage C organism is more robust at that dose but breaks down soon after. They frame WtS as an elicitation attack, not as a test of weak-to-strong generalization.
record.recipe_differences: It fine-tunes a stronger model organism on a weaker model's answers, but uses this as an elicitation attack on hard vulnerability samples, with only 2 training steps, and reports hard-sample recall rather than PGR against a true-label-trained ceiling.
record.method_sensitivity: The result varies substantially across starting model organisms; the paper also plots hard recall across WtS training steps in Figure 3d and says the final organism breaks down soon after the tested dose.
record.problems: The paper does not calculate PGR or report a strong ceiling trained on true labels, so it does not directly establish the claim's normalized gap-recovery result. The WtS comparison uses one vulnerability task and one weak/strong model pairing; Table 4 gives no uncertainty intervals for the reported recall values.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3d plots recall across training steps for Stage A, Stage B, and Stage C, but the text does not provide exact plotted values; its trend is summarized in method_sensitivity and authors_conclusion rather than assigned approximate values.

untested.parts: PGR against a strong ceiling trained on true labels; tasks other than code-vulnerability detection; more than one weak/strong pair.
All parts: no training-method variants for improving WtS.
All parts: one supervisor/student size pair and one task; no analysis of what predicts gains.
All parts in the original sense. Stage C was trained specifically to resist WtS, which is adversarial, not a natural failure mode.

missing.what: Easy-sample recall after WtS training. B scores 88.4%, below T's baseline easy recall (90.5%) and T's WtS easy recall (95.2%). Stage A–C score 90.5/94.6/96.6%. On easy items the strong student does not clearly beat the weak supervisor.
Hard recall across WtS training steps (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16) for Stage A–C, including the text's claim that even one step elicits nonzero recall and that Stage C breaks down soon after 2 steps.

record.verdict_notes: There is a text inconsistency. Section 3.4 says WtS trains U on T's responses on Dtest,hard, while the Table 4 caption and Section 5.3 say Dtrain,hard. If the test split was used, the results would be contaminated; the rows assume the train split. Hard items were filtered to those T solves at most 1/6 times, so T's training responses are mostly incorrect, and students exceeding T reflects either recovering suppressed capability or general reversion. No true-label ceiling or PGR is computed. Table 4 reports no intervals, although Appendix D mentions bootstrap CIs. Each cell pools 3 samples over 51 hard items. Stage C was trained via TAR specifically to resist this attack, so its result reflects adversarial design rather than a natural limit of weak-to-strong generalization.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not calculate PGR, establish a strong ceiling using true-label training, or test the usual weak-to-strong generalization setup apart from its vulnerability-task elicitation attack.

rows.subject: T (Qwen3-8B)
rows.operation_detail: Supervisor's hard-sample recall under baseline elicitation; reference for the WtS-trained students.
rows.note: The paper identifies T as the human-proxy weaker model. Table 4 reports 7.8% hard recall for T under baseline elicitation.
rows.check: Supervisor reference row, not an effect. T's own recall under the WtS protocol is 11.1% (Table 4); students could also be compared against that figure.

rows.subject: B (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on T's responses to hard vulnerability samples.
rows.note: The WtS-trained model's hard recall exceeds T's 7.8% baseline, although it is below B's own 71.2% baseline. Table 4 says each cell pools three samples per item.
rows.check: Baseline 71.2% is B's own untrained recall, which acts as the strong reference, not the comparator for V1. The comparator is T's 7.8%. This is the setup closest to the original: B falls from 71.2% to 23.5%, staying above T. With B's own recall as ceiling, the implied PGR is about 0.25, an approximation only, since there is no true-label ceiling.
